faq: Will this get my plugin accepted on WordPress.org?
We cannot promise acceptance, because the plugin team reviews the code and the listing. We write to their guidelines and avoid wording that commonly causes delays or removal.
Can you write reviews for the listing?
No. We do not write, buy or swap reviews, and doing so breaks WordPress.org rules. Reviews have to come from real users of your plugin.
Do you need my plugin code?
A zip or a test site is enough for most listings, so we describe features accurately. We may ask a few questions about settings and limits to avoid claims the plugin cannot keep.
Can you write for a paid marketplace instead?
Yes. Tell us which marketplace and we follow its length limits and image sizes. Paid marketplaces allow more selling language than WordPress.org, while still banning misleading claims.
desc:
A WordPress.org and marketplace plugin listing is the page where store owners decide whether to install your plugin. Ecom Swift LLC writes the readme, names, descriptions and FAQ, and prepares screenshots, icon and banner in the format those directories expect.

## What is a WordPress.org plugin listing?

It is the public page for your plugin, built mainly from a file called readme.txt that follows a set format. The file holds the plugin name, short description, long description, installation steps, FAQ and changelog. The images, such as the icon, banner and screenshots, are uploaded separately.

Paid marketplaces use a similar structure with their own fields and limits. The text is what both people and search engines read when deciding if your plugin solves their problem.

## Why does a listing matter for installs?

A store owner searching for a plugin sees a name, an icon and one short line. If the line is vague, they move on. If the page opens with a clear sentence about what the plugin does and who it is for, they keep reading.

A poorly written listing also causes wrong installs. People who expected a different feature leave bad ratings and send support tickets. A precise description attracts the right users and filters out the wrong ones, which saves your support time.

## How listing quality affects discovery

Directory search matches words in your name, short description and tags. Using the phrases store owners really type helps your plugin appear for the right searches. It works best when those phrases appear in natural sentences, not in a stuffed list.

Screenshots matter because many visitors scan images before reading text. Captions that explain what each screen shows turn a gallery into a mini tour. A clear banner and icon make the listing look maintained.

## What a great plugin listing includes

- A plugin name that says what the plugin does, with alternatives to choose from.
- A short description that fits the directory length limit and states the main benefit.
- A long description that opens with the problem, then lists features in plain words.
- Installation steps written for a store owner, not a developer.
- A FAQ that answers real pre-install questions.
- A changelog in the expected format.
- Tags and search terms matched to real searches.
- Captioned screenshots in a sensible order.
- A support policy that tells users where to ask for help.
- An icon and banner in the required sizes.

## What we do

We read your plugin and ask what it does for a store owner, who it is for and what makes it different. We draft name options and the short description first, since those shape everything else. Then we write the full readme, check its format and compare it with the published plugin guidelines.

For packages that include images, we create captioned screenshots, an icon in two sizes and a banner, and prepare the files for upload to your account. Higher packages add a free and Pro comparison and a demo video script. We write only honest text: no invented reviews, no ranking claims and no hidden upsells. We can also adapt the text for a paid marketplace page.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Describe the one problem your plugin solves in the first sentence.
- Use screenshots that show the real settings screen and real results.
- Explain clearly what is free and what needs an upgrade.
- Keep the changelog current with each release.
- Answer support questions where the listing says you will.

**Avoid:**
- Naming other brands in your title to borrow their search traffic.
- Asking users for reviews inside the listing text.
- Hiding that a feature belongs to a paid version.
- Filling tags with unrelated words.
- Using screenshots of a mock-up that your plugin does not match.

## Who this service is for

This service suits a developer who built a useful plugin but finds writing hard. It suits an agency that wants to release a client tool to the public directory. It also suits a team preparing a first release who want the listing checked against the guidelines before submitting.

## What we need from you

Send the plugin zip or a clear feature list, access to a test site or screenshots of the main screens, and any brand colors. You do not need to share live store passwords, and we never ask for them. Acceptance and ranking are decided by the directory, so we focus on a clear, honest listing that follows its rules.
